The Methods Hub aims to provide social scientists with high-quality, open-access, and easy-to-use computational resources for:

- **data collection**
- **preprocessing**
- **data analysis**
- **data visualization**
- **validation and evaluation**
- **computational workflows**

A special focus of the Methods Hub is on resources that work on [digital behavioral data](https://www.gesis.org/en/institute/about-us/digital-behavioral-data), but other resources are also welcome.

With this, we want to promote the use of computational methods in the social sciences, lower technical barriers, and build a community-driven space for the field. We also offer [interactive execution environments](#interactive-env) so everyone can try methods and tutorials with a single click. For contributors, we provide a platform where they can reach their community. Every published item on the Methods Hub gets a DOI, making the resources citable.

## Our Mission

We collect high-quality, open-access computational methods.

We promote the use of computational methods in social science by lowering technical barriers.

We are building a community-driven hub of methods—by researchers, for researchers.

We curate tools that support reproducible workflows.

We provide visibility for your methods—consider submitting!

We offer interactive execution environments so everyone can try the methods with the click of a button.


## What you can publish and why should submit to the Methods Hub

Publishing on the Methods Hub makes your work visible to the computational social science community and easy for researchers to find, run, and adapt. Readers can try your method directly in an interactive environment without any setup, which lowers the barrier for researchers who are new to computational methods. Your work also becomes part of a curated collection that supports transparent and reproducible research.

Further, everything published on the Methods Hub receives a DOI, which makes your method or tutorial citable! This way, the time you invest in documenting and sharing your code counts as a recognised scholarly contribution that others can reference in their work.

The Methods Hub welcomes two kinds of contributions:

A **method** on the Methods Hub is a computational procedure that can be employed to address social science problems. It is published in a code repository, encompassing scripts, packages, libraries, or notebooks, and follows our guidelines – most importantly, being reusable, free, and open source software (FOSS).

For example, you can submit an R package for preprocessing social media data. For details on how to prepare a method, see the [Method Template](https://methodshub.gesis.org/).

[TODO: add example methods]

A **tutorial** on the Methods Hub is a written, recorded, and/or interactive introduction to a workflow, tool, or one or more methods. It is an instructional resource that can be used for self-guided learning.

Tutorials should focus on concrete tasks and offer code that helps researchers solve them (e.g., how to preprocess data for topic modeling). They may apply methods featured on the Methods Hub, but can also refer to methods published elsewhere, and a tutorial can feature more than one method. For details on how to prepare a tutorial, see the [Tutorial Template](https://methodshub.gesis.org/).

## What makes us special: 

### Interactive environments {#interactive-env}

To ensure an exploratory user experience, we prefer methods and tutorials that include interactive elements, where users can modify one or more parameters and see how their changes affect the script's behavior. For this, we integrate so-called **interactive environments**.

An interactive environment is a ready-to-use computing session that opens directly in the browser. Users don't need to install software, set up packages, or download data. With one click, they can run the code, change parameters, and explore the results themselves. This makes methods accessible to researchers who are new to programming and lets experienced users quickly test whether a method fits their own research question.

For contributors, this means that your submission should run from top to bottom in a fresh environment. All dependencies need to be declared, data needs to be included or openly accessible, and runtimes should stay reasonably short. We have more details on this in our [submission checklist](https://methodshub.gesis.org/)

We also gathered some tips to help you optimize your method or tutorial for a great [interactive user experience](https://methodshub.gesis.org/).

### Taxonomy

To help users find what they need, every submission is classified using a shared [taxonomy](https://methodshub.gesis.org/submit/taxonomy/). Contributions are further tagged by keywords and programming language, so that users can browse the Methods Hub by what they want to do rather than by tool names they may not yet know. When you submit, you assign your contribution to the relevant categories, and our team reviews the classification.

### Making Methods Citable

Developing and documenting a method takes considerable time, but software and tutorials often go unrecognised in academic careers. The Methods Hub addresses this: every published method and tutorial receives a DOI, together with citation information drawn from your `CITATION.cff` file. Others can cite your work just like a journal article, and your contribution becomes visible as a scholarly output in its own right.

### From the Community to the Community

The Methods Hub is built by and for the computational social science community. Contributions come from researchers who have developed, adapted, or taught a method and want others to benefit from it. In turn, users can build on these contributions, adapt them to new contexts, and share their own work. Our goal is a growing, curated collection that reflects the diversity of methods in the field and lowers the barrier to using them well.
